Census reconciles exactly: 18 clean = 40 candidate lines - 16 inside $(...) - 6 named exclusions; 19 with one mutation; 21 with both (selfcheck:85 is two &&-joined segments). Verified at dd7026f8 from the agent worktree, log carries the path: cargo test --workspace 4551/0/2 exit 0 with the new test's ok line IN it, clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings exit 0, nightly_source_gates.sh --audit unclassified=0. SKIP-TEXT-HOLE is STALE - closed 2026-08-27 (c1718cb2 via df21c18f): skip_marker_lint holds every announced early return to one marker via two independent detectors, the nightly script EXTRACTS the marker rather than retyping it, landing-run.sh and refreeze.rs count both spellings, and the 30 remaining 'skipping' hits are prose. Recommend closing the booking. LEFT OPEN: pipelines inside $(...) are not read by the lint at all - correct under set -uo pipefail, a hole under set -e with zero instances today that stops being zero the moment anyone adds -e to a script holding a $(... | head).

headline: We are the ones silently accepting a broken program - the old assembler refuses it and we do not.
matters: I sent an agent to find out what the RIGHT answer is for a construct I believed both copies of the old assembler got wrong. The answer came back inverted. On the shape that matters, the old assembler is correct and WE are the ones quietly accepting nonsense: write a call to a little formula that ignores its argument, hand it a name that was never defined anywhere, and the old assembler stops and says 'symbol undefined'. We emit code. I ran both myself to be sure. The cause is that we skip evaluating an argument when the formula does not use it - which sounds like a harmless optimisation and means a program referencing something that does not exist assembles clean. Nothing in the games hits this today: zero sites across all four codebases, 2,056 files. So it is a latent soundness hole rather than a live bug, and the fix is small and well-evidenced - the assembler's own manual says arguments are always evaluated. Also worth knowing: the old assembler stops reporting undefined symbols after its first error of any kind, and says so in tiny print at the bottom of the listing that nobody reads. Any test file of ours with several deliberate errors may have been under-reporting. That is now booked and three runners detect it.
detail: master 932c93be, merge 6df982c5, docs-only. 33 shapes one per file, both assemblers, controls in band: asl silent on 16, loud on 17. Boundary established by four refuting probes - silent set is exactly a0-a7/d0-d7/sp (pc/sr/ccr/usp/a1.w loud); body-uses-parameter irrelevant to asl; one '+' makes it loud; 68000-only since z80 register names are not expression symbols. RIGHT ANSWER IS REFUSE on five sources outside the binaries: AS's manual documents FUNCTION as strict with textual insertion of int/float/string; as.msg already carries 'expected integer, floating point number or string but got register'; the shipped source shows the bail is a MISSING WrError with three of four early exits in that loop reporting; upstream removed the mechanism and added an explicit TempReg case; dc.w a1 carries an upstream assert marked unreachable that two of four builds abort on. VERIFIED AT THIS SEAT: move.w #fi(zz),d0 with fi ignoring its parameter and zz undefined - asl exit 2 error #1010, sigil exit 0 emitting 30 3C 03 C7. Sigil refuses 31 of 33 and beats every asl build on 15 of the 16 silent shapes; the two it accepts share ONE cause, lazy argument expansion. Corpus zero: 2,056 .asm across s1disasm/s2disasm/skdisasm/aeon, 116 function defs, 0 param-ignoring, 0 #name(reg), 0 dc.x reg; s2disasm's 289 id(aN) all peeled addressing modes. Row is mis-booked as one construct - it is asl's silent decline (nearly closed) and sigil's lazy expansion (the actual defect), intersecting at one shape. ALSO CORRECTED, mine: the instrument count was wrong twice. 'Four binaries' became 'four paths two programs' and that correction was itself a sample. Measured by running every asl on the machine with file(1): SEVEN paths execute under FOUR digests, the reference reached by three paths, and s2disasm/build_tools/Linux-x86/asl is an ELF 64-bit binary in the 32-bit slot with its own digest - selecting by architecture directory gets a program neither path nor banner describes. Guard unaffected; it pins one digest and refuses three. Fixed in OVERSEER.md and the asl-reference README at 932c93be.

headline: The explanation I gave this morning for that silent-failure bug was itself wrong, and the wrong version was the more dangerous one. Corrected, with the correct rule measured.
matters: This morning I correctly showed that the bug can happen on an idle machine, not just a busy one. But I then said the wrong thing about WHY: I said being busy makes it more likely. It does not. What decides it is how much the writing program still has left to say after the searching program has already found what it wanted. If the writer has already finished, the bug is impossible. If the writer still has more to push out, the bug is near-certain. Being busy only matters in the narrow gap between those. That matters far more than the thing it replaces, because my version told people that a check running alone, once a night, was the low-risk case - and the truth is the exact opposite: a nightly job scanning a large amount of material is in the near-certain zone. The coordinator caught this. I measured it myself before accepting it, and found their proposed rule of thumb was also off - by about eight times in the unsafe direction for the kind of writer our scripts actually use. All the earlier numbers stay; they were real, they just meant something different. I also found and fixed a flaw in the new automatic check: it was reading the build folder, where other tests create their own throwaway scripts, so it could have failed because of what an unrelated test was doing.
detail: Coordinator challenge accepted and independently reproduced. SIZE, not concurrency, is the governing variable: boundary.sh, ONE worker, no concurrency, bash printf writer, needle on line 1 -> 0/400 at 4798 bytes, 4/400 at 7198, 83/400 at 9598, 287/400 at 10798, 394/400 at 14398, 400/400 at 23998. My 'load AMPLIFIES it ~44x' is struck in place per this lane's CORRECTED convention. BUT THEIR STATED BOUNDARY IS ALSO WRONG AND WRONG IN THE PERMISSIVE DIRECTION: three writers over the SAME 65536-byte pipe (F_GETPIPE_SZ read, not assumed) turn over at wildly different sizes - printf 4798->14398 (BELOW the pipe), seq 23998->239998, cat 479998->719998. A boundary moving 100x on a fixed pipe is not the pipe's; what governs is the writer's own output buffering (that explanation is inference, no strace; the turnovers are measured). 'Under a pipe buffer therefore safe' would clear a bash-builtin writer at 9598 bytes measuring 83/400. Usable rule = the smallest turnover: a shell-builtin writer with more than a few KB past the earliest match is near-certain. RECONCILES both measurements rather than replacing one: the founding site's writer is ~1.1 KB (racing band), which is exactly why 9600 concurrent showed 44 and serial 4000 showed none. Also, at base rate 1/9600, zero in 4000 has p=0.66 - the modal outcome. VERDICT RE-READ, all 39 sites: NONE changed; two REASONS did, both mine (selfcheck.sh:85 'short message = widest window' is backwards, it is the RARE band; ci.yml 'latent below a pipe buffer' priced by a number the step exists to let grow). The other 37 ride on (c) or on structure, untouched. SHARPENED: REGISTER=$(sed|grep -v|head -20) at nightly_source_gates.sh:620 is fed by a grep -v streaming the whole suite log - near-certain regime, runs once serially - and is safe ONLY because there is no set -e. I claimed the lint would catch that transition, TESTED it instead of asserting, and was WRONG: mutating -e in reds line 233 but NOT 620, which lives inside $(...) where the lint does not read. Anyone fixing the flagged line alone would believe the file was clear - the founding failure shape one level up - so the $(...) hole is promoted from residual to first item to close. LINT DEFECT FOUND WHILE RE-VERIFYING (mine): it walked the disk into .cargo-target, where other harness tests plant bed shell scripts, so it could red on another test's activity; population is now git ls-files with a loud refusal, units 84->85, runtime 5.54s->0.02s. Red-first re-proved AFTER the population swap (baselines taken from master, not HEAD - HEAD now holds the fixes and handed me the fixed file the first time). Verified at this branch tip: cargo test --workspace 4551/0/2 exit 0 with the new test's ok line IN the log, clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings exit 0 with zero finding lines, nightly_source_gates.sh --audit unclassified=0.

headline: The automatic check I shipped this morning was giving WRONG answers, not merely incomplete ones - it could tell you a file was clean when it was not. Closed, and while measuring it I found my own explanation of the bug was wrong for the fourth time.
matters: This morning's check looks for a silent bug where a program reports 'not found' when the answer was 'found'. It could not see inside one very common way of writing shell - capturing a command's output into a variable. That is worse than not having the check at all: if you added the risky setting to one of our scripts, the check would point at ONE line and stay silent about a SECOND one right below it, so whoever fixed the line it named would watch the check go green and reasonably conclude the file was clear. That is the same failure the whole effort exists to stop, one level up. It now sees inside those, and I proved it by writing a fault the old check was green on and the new one is red on. Two other things worth knowing. First, I checked the rule against the shell itself rather than trusting my memory of it, and my memory would have been wrong in BOTH directions - one error would have made the check cry wolf until someone switched it off, the other would have made it silently miss real bugs. That comparison against the real shell now runs every time. Second, I measured the one site the morning's note called 'near-certain to break': it is in fact impossible to break today, because the note mis-read which program was doing the writing. The conclusion does not change - it is still a defect waiting to happen, for a reason that has nothing to do with size - but that is now four different explanations of this bug that turned out to be wrong, and not one of them ever changed a single ruling.
detail: PIPEFAIL-CMDSUBST-HOLE, branch parcel/pipefail-cmdsubst-hole off a8d3c5c1. HOLE CONFIRMED FIRSTHAND, not inherited: `sed -i 29s/set -uo/set -euo/` on nightly_source_gates.sh, lint AS COMMITTED names line 233 only and misses 620 `REGISTER=$(sed -n RANGE | grep -v | head -20)`. Closed by a substitution scanner that reads `$( )` INSIDE double quotes (the old top_level_positions skipped all quoted text), steps over `$(( ))`, recurses, and scans backticks (this tree has none - all 37 backtick lines are prose in quoted strings or a sed pattern, enumerated - so scanning them keeps the lint off that snapshot). POSITION RULE MEASURED AGAINST BASH, and the previously-booked guess ('is the substitution the whole assignment RHS') is wrong in both directions: `x="pre $(exit 7)"` propagates (7) so concatenation does not stop it, and `local x=$(exit 7)` does NOT (0) because the declaration builtin's own status masks it - as do export/declare/readonly; argument position does not propagate. That table is now a standing test that RUNS BASH and compares, because both errors are silent on a clean corpus. Consumption model UNCHANGED (if/elif/while/until/!, && gating, bare under set -e); two censuses counted separately (18 top-level, 10 in `$( )`) each with its own COULD NOT MEASURE, since one shared total is how this lint shipped blind. UNDECIDABLE CASES, direction chosen and stated: a function's LAST statement hands its status out (measured: plain assignment tail -> 7, local tail -> 0) and set -e can arrive from a sourcer; NOT flagged, because flagging them means flagging every v=$(...|head -1) on the theory some caller might read the status - about two dozen findings on a clean tree, an always-red check that gets fixed by weakening it. The counts that make that a measurement: ZERO of the ten substitution sites is a function tail, and the whole tree has ONE function-tail instance (reference_env_var:233, top-level, already cleared by caller enumeration in the earlier sweep). `||` as a consumer recorded not adopted: zero findings today. RED-FIRST x4, each shown on disk: (M1) propagates->true = model test RED with 8 named disagreements while THE CORPUS GATE STAYED GREEN, which is why it is a separate instrument; (M2) propagates->false + the set -e mutation = corpus gate reverts to exactly the pre-parcel answer, model test RED with 4; (M3) scanner returns empty = COULD NOT MEASURE on sub_census; (M4) nightly_ref_drift.sh:276 rewritten as `if READS_PATTERN=$(...|head -1)` with NO set -e anywhere = OLD lint (git show HEAD:) GREEN, NEW lint RED. M4 is the bar this parcel was set. Restores from md5-verified copy (ac383365) or git show HEAD:, never git checkout -- on a dirty tree. RE-RUN ON THE CLEAN TREE: zero findings; new surface adds 10 to the census and 0 to the offences; all ten enumerated with (c) and a band, none narrowed. MEASUREMENT CORRECTING THE MORNING NOTE: site 620 priced as 'squarely near-certain' is IMPOSSIBLE today - construct lifted from the file, 200 runs per bed, K register rows: K=2 0/200, K=19 0/200 (head -20 never even fills), K=20-25 0/200 (head exits, grep had finished), K=100 19/200, K=5000 200/200. Two errors: `sed -n '/A/,/B/p'` READS the whole log and WRITES only the range, so the writer is bounded by the register block; and CORPUS_OPEN_FINDINGS holds 2 rows so head -20 never exits early. Verdict unchanged and held up by the note's own rule - a register of open findings exists in order to grow. NEW INSTRUMENT writers_grep_sed.sh: boundary.sh measured printf/seq/cat into grep -q and NOT ONE of the ten sites uses any of those; grep/sed/awk/builtin into head -20 over the same kernel-read 65536-byte pipe give last-0%/first-95% of 3100/62000, 3100/124000, 3100/31000, 651/18600. Size mechanism HOLDS (monotone, serial, four different turnovers on one pipe) but the '~100x spread' is a property of which writers and which reader, not a constant: these four sit inside one order and straddle the pipe. Working rule for this tree: >3KB owed past the exit is at risk, >60KB near-certain, whatever the writer. FOUR MECHANISM STORIES NOW (load gates it / load amplifies it / the pipe is the boundary / the whole log is the writer) and NOT ONE ever changed a verdict - every ruling rests on (a) and (c), readable in a second. VERIFICATION at 081fcb61, log stamped with pwd/HEAD/branch: cargo test --workspace exit 0, 4553 passed 0 failed 2 ignored (4551+2, reconciles), zero FAILED lines, all three new/changed tests named ok in that log; clippy plain AND -D warnings both exit 0 with zero error/warning lines (plain reported too, because -D stops at the first finding and would size the problem as 'one'); nightly_source_gates.sh --audit exit 0, SOURCE_GATES=46 scanned=138 source=45 artifact=87 no-reference=6 unclassified=0, unchanged. LEFT OPEN: the two escape routes above; `||`; two assignment shapes bash propagates through and the position rule rejects (`b=$(...) a=1`, `arr=( $(...) )`, neither present here, both named in the code); a `$( )` split across physical lines by something no continuation rule folds, which would be read truncated and fail silently.

headline: Fixed the check I shipped this morning that could tell you a file was clean when it was not - and four explanations for that bug have now fallen without one of them ever mattering.
matters: The check I landed earlier today had a blind spot: it flagged one risky line and missed another two hundred lines away, so anyone who fixed what it pointed at would have watched it go green and stopped looking. That is worse than not having the check for those places, which is why it jumped the queue ahead of new work. It is closed, and I proved the fix does something real rather than trusting the report - I broke a file in a way the OLD check could not see, confirmed the old one passes it and the new one catches it by name. The interesting part is a piece of shell behaviour nobody had measured. Whether this bug can bite depends on a subtle rule about when a failure inside a command actually reaches the surrounding script, and the guess we had written down was wrong in BOTH directions at once - too narrow in one case, too broad in another. That is now a test that runs the real shell and compares, because being wrong either way leaves no trace on a working system. And the honest headline: there have now been FOUR competing explanations for what makes this bug fire - two of them mine - and not one of them ever changed a single verdict. Every decision rested on two simple structural questions. The theorising was decoration on a procedure that never used it.
detail: master a1df90c1, merge of parcel/pipefail-cmdsubst-hole (46cb6173). Full strict suite on the MERGED tree with the provisioned reference tree: 398 binaries, 4553 passed, 0 failed, 2 ignored, zero partial-run disclosures, the lint named in the run's own log; clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings clean. VERIFIED AT THIS SEAT rather than accepted: (1) the bash table, bash -c 'set -e; f(){ STMT; echo REACHED; }; f' - x=$(exit 7) does not reach, x="pre $(exit 7)" does not reach (concatenation does NOT stop propagation), local x=$(exit 7) REACHES, export the same, argument position REACHES; so the booked rule 'substitution is the whole assignment RHS' was wrong in both directions and the implemented rule is a PLAIN assignment with the substitution anywhere in its value. (2) The red-first bar, which is the right one - a mutation the OLD lint would have missed: nightly_ref_drift.sh:276 rewritten as `if READS_PATTERN=$(… | head -1); then :; fi` with no set -e anywhere, mutation confirmed on disk by grep and git diff --stat, master's lint md5-matched to the master blob exits GREEN, this branch's exits RED naming the line; both restored from committed baselines. The agent also refuted MY pricing in its brief: I called site 620 near-certain because its writer 'streams the whole suite log'; sed -n '/A/,/B/p' READS the whole log and WRITES only the range, and head -20 never exits until it has 20 lines, which that register's 2 rows never supply - 200 runs per bed, K=2 0/200, K=100 19/200, K=5000 200/200, so the site is IMPOSSIBLE today and the verdict is unchanged for a different reason. Undecidable cases decided by a count not a preference: flagging them costs ~24 findings on a clean tree, an always-red check that gets fixed by being weakened, and zero of the ten substitution sites is a function tail. Left open: two escape routes, || as a consumer (zero findings today), two shapes bash propagates through that the position rule rejects, and a $(…) split across lines no continuation rule folds.

headline: The assembler now refuses all 33 of the shapes we tested, including the one where we were emitting code for a program that names a symbol nobody defined.
matters: This closes the soundness hole from earlier today. We were accepting a program that referred to something that does not exist, because we skipped evaluating an argument the formula did not use. Now we evaluate it, and the refusal names the missing symbol - the same words we already used for the case that did work. A register handed where a value belongs now gets its own message saying so, instead of claiming you forgot to define it. Nothing in any of the four codebases changes: 1,702 assembly files produce byte-identical output before and after. The part I want to keep is how that null result was made trustworthy. 1,702 files agreeing is exactly what you would also see if the sweep accidentally ran the same binary twice - so the sweep refuses to start unless the OLD binary accepts the bad program and the NEW one rejects it. That guard also quietly solves a problem this lane keeps hitting: on a change that moves no bytes, matching results cannot prove the build actually ran. Here they can, because a stale build would still accept and the sweep would not start. Half-done and booked, not glossed: the same mistake still produces a misleading message on one variant, and fixing it properly needs a wider change than this parcel should carry.
detail: master d5b5e8f1, merge of parcel/as-strict-function-args (e335efb9). Strict suite on the MERGED tree with AEON_DIR provisioned: 399 binaries, 4558 passed, 0 failed, 2 ignored, zero partial-run disclosures, the new test named in the log; clippy clean. All three grounds I ruled on re-verified by the parcel: confined to crates/sigil-frontend-as/src/eval.rs with .emp's evaluator untouched; zero AS function definitions in aeon's three routed .asm files, both ROM shapes rebuilt with the post-change assembler MATCHING THE GOLDEN and pins.rs unchanged; corpus population zero. Diagnostics verified at this seat through the committed instrument: #fi(zz) -> 'unresolved symbol `zz` in operand' (verbatim what #fu(zz) already said, the landing condition), #fi(a1) -> '`a1` is a register: a function argument must be an integer, floating point number or string'. RESIDUE BOOKED as AS-REGISTER-DIAGNOSTIC-RESIDUE: #fu(a1), where the body USES the parameter, still says 'unresolved symbol `a1`' - correct refusal, misleading message; closing it needs an &mut cascade through the string-builtin subtree and half-way prints two diagnostics for one operand. DEVIATION RATIFIED: my brief said evaluate EVERY argument; the agent flagged that a used parameter's argument is already calculated by substitution so checking it again doubles the diagnostic, and delivered the rule by checking exactly the ignored ones - right rule, corrected implementation, stated rather than done quietly. ALSO MEASURED FOR THE OWNER, at his question: s1disasm (f6ece65) 57 diagnostics, s2disasm (e45ebf3) 5761, via `sigil sonic.asm` and `sigil s2.asm` from each corpus dir. Identical at session boot (ba94655a, built in a detached worktree) - today's seven parcels moved the corpus count by ZERO, six touching no assembler code and the seventh closing a construct with no corpus instances. s2's top blocks: 2624 bad-operand-expression, 2309 expected-mnemonic-directive-or-label, 518 bad-absolute-address (AS-JMPTOS-518-BLOCK, all from s2.macrosetup.asm:304). AS-Z80-INSTRUCTION-COVERAGE contributes 0 to this count - different entry path.

headline: Sonic 2's two biggest assembler complaints are not two problems. They are one missing feature, and it accounts for 86 percent of everything the assembler says about that game.
matters: We were about to plan work off two big numbers as though they were two jobs. They are four different messages coming out of one cause: the old assembler lets you write a throwaway label as a bare plus or minus sign and jump to it, and we do not support that at all. Not partly, not with gaps. Zero of the five thousand places it is used. Everything left over after that cause is accounted for is zero, and that was proved by matching every single line to a rule rather than by subtracting one number from another. One warning I have written into the record in strong terms: you cannot subtract this from the total to predict what the count will be after we fix it. Fixing it lets the assembler reach code it currently gives up on, so the number can go down and up at the same time. The only way to know is to measure after.
detail: AS-S2-TOP-BLOCKS-DECOMPOSE, measure only, no crate touched. Landed 49acd05d. RC-1 = AS nameless temporary labels (+, -, /). 4,985 rows across 4 message classes, 86.5 percent of the 5,761 row run. Residual 0 rows / 0 sites in both subject classes via positive match rule, OTHER bucket written to file. d-22 ruled accept 2026-09-03; 0 of 5,003 constructs accepted. s1-path-to-rom.md:400 is incomplete not wrong, booking only the definition half, understating 2.2x. Overseer corroborated by a different instrument (corpus-side source count with sigil out of the loop): 2,339 definitions, 2,711 references, slightly more than sigil reports, the honest direction. Note at docs/superpowers/notes/2026-09-05-s2-top-blocks-decompose.md, re-runnable probes beside it.

headline: A reference tool we quote numbers from can hand back a wrong value for a line that assembled fine, if anything else in the same file failed. Now written into the rules.
matters: We check that we are running the right copy of the old assembler, because there are seven copies on this machine and they do not all behave the same. That check is not enough. If a file has even one bad line somewhere, an unrelated correct line elsewhere in it can come back with a corrupted answer, and the printout looks complete. In the case that found this, a jump instruction came back pointing at itself instead of where it should go. The dangerous part is that the wrong value looked completely reasonable: right shape, right size, nothing to notice. Anyone who had quoted it would have been quoting a fabricated number while having followed every rule we had written down. There are now two checks instead of one: which program ran, and whether its answers mean anything.
detail: Found by the S2 decomposition parcel against its own probe (bra.s / invalid, / is definition-only in AS); a macro-expanded beq.s + returned 67FE instead of 6702. Banked in docs/OVERSEER.md beside the md5 ruling at 52a66719. Verified here that asl_ref.sh checks the binary and not the run: all four exit sites select the digest. Booked ASL-GUARD-EXIT-STATUS; until it lands, exit-status checking is the caller's job.

headline: The dashes are gone from everything the tools say to a person, and a check now stops them coming back.
matters: Your instruction is done for this tool: 1,133 pieces of text changed, across the assembler's messages, its help, and the shell and Python tools beside it. The thing that makes it safe to accept a change that size without reading every line is one rule: every single edit had to be punctuation only. Strip the punctuation out of the old and new text and the letters must be identical. That was checked mechanically across all of it, with no exceptions. It matters because more than five hundred of those pieces of text are quoted inside tests, and the tempting way to fix a test that goes red is to paste in whatever the tool now says, which would hide a message that had stopped appearing at all. Nothing was pasted; one function moved the tool's words and the tests' expectations together. There is now a permanent check that fails the build if a dash comes back, and I proved at my own desk that it really fires rather than just being green.
detail: TOOLTEXT-DASH-SWEEP landed f6618ec9, ruling and lessons 7b260a63, pushed. 1,012 Rust string literals (494 producer, 518 consumer) + 43 Python + 78 shell. Punctuation-only gate: 270 files, 1,168 paired lines, 0 deviations. Gate crates/sigil-harness/tests/tool_text_dash_lint.rs in cargo test --workspace; lexes rather than greps (10,887 comment dashes vs 1,012 string). Re-proved red-first on the MERGED tree at the overseer seat, both directions: a dash in a real string literal reds and names file:line; a dash in a comment correctly does not. Suite 4,560 passed / 0 failed / exit 0, clippy clean. Stated plainly: 371 passing rows are reference-dependent and measured nothing, byte-identity golden gates among them, not run.

headline: I got the same simple count wrong three times today, and the agent I sent refused my number instead of matching it.
matters: I measured how many pieces of text needed changing and reported it to you twice. Both figures were wrong. The first came back as zero because my search pattern matched no files at all, which looks exactly like a clean result. The next two were inflated because the counting program I wrote could not tell a piece of text from a comment: the assembler's own source contains a quote mark inside quote marks, and my counter lost its place there and never recovered, so it counted hundreds of comments as text and, worse, missed real text after that point. The agent doing the work measured it itself, got a different answer, and said so plainly rather than quietly reconciling to what I had told it. That is the behaviour I want and it is worth recording. What settled it was running a corrected counter over both versions and getting 1,031 before and 0 after, matching the agent's independent count exactly.
detail: 582 then 595 reported; true occurrence count 1,031. Cause: hand-rolled Rust lexer with no char-literal state, desynced by b'"' at sigil-frontend-as/src/eval.rs:2208. Error is bidirectional: after a desync real strings read as code and are missed. Banked in docs/OVERSEER.md with the rule (when a count needs a lexer, use a real one or prove it against a second method) plus two more: a control is what makes a count mean anything, and my own brief carried a contradictory CARGO_TARGET_DIR instruction that cost the agent two suite runs because only .target-land satisfies both guards.

headline: The third biggest Sonic 2 complaint block is closed. It was two separate faults, and neither was the one I had diagnosed.
matters: 518 complaints, all from one line of Sonic 2's jump table generator, are now zero, and nothing else moved: no other kind of complaint appeared or increased, checked line by line rather than by comparing totals. The part worth telling you is that I diagnosed this myself before handing it over, and I was wrong twice. My test for the first fault was built on an off by one: I asked for a piece of text starting at the wrong position, got the wrong name, and read the resulting failure as proof of the thing I already suspected. My test could not have told the difference. The second fault was real but I described it far too narrowly, and the narrow version would have produced a fix that made the 518 complaints vanish while leaving the same underlying fault broken everywhere else, with the count dropping to zero and appearing to prove it. The agent measured both, refused my account, and said so plainly. That question I put at the end of every brief, asking what in it was wrong, has now found something four times out of four.
detail: AS-JMPTOS-518-BLOCK landed c325c7a2, lessons 3a311a9c, pushed. Corpus 5,761 rows/5,113 sites to 5,243/5,112; bad absolute address expression 518 to 0; diagnostic multiset diffed line by line, 0 lines present after but not before; unresolved symbol name sets equal in both directions. Defect 1: AS substr is 0-based, my probe used offset 7 giving "oo"; real fault was fold_const not expanding nested string builtins in substr's pos/len. Defect 2: no 68000 instruction operand ran any builtin layer at all; move.l #int(3.7),d0 fails on master with nothing string-shaped in it. Both refutations verified firsthand at this seat. Red-first re-proved on the merged tree. Byte gates did NOT execute, 127 reference-dependent binaries unmeasured; covered instead by an inertness argument with a falsifier.

headline: The assembler was silently accepting a real mistake. Writing a register where a number belongs was quietly ignored in any file that already had an error, which is every file people actually work on.
matters: This started as a tidy-up: the same mistake produced different error messages depending on where you made it, and I wanted one clear message. It turned out one of those cases produced NO message at all. Writing a processor register where a number belongs was simply swallowed, and it only behaves that way once something else in the file has already gone wrong, which is exactly the situation you are in when you are fixing errors. I proved it by putting the mistake into the real Sonic 2 source at a known line: the old assembler produced 5,243 complaints and not one of them mentioned that line. It now names the line and says plainly that you used a register. Two other silent faults were found alongside it and written down: one construct crashes the assembler outright, and another quietly evaluates as false rather than complaining.
detail: AS-REGISTER-DIAGNOSTIC-RESIDUE landed 4b6e0378, lesson b273071b, pushed. Booked as 2 stories, dispatched by me as 3 after reproducing, delivered as 7 outcomes including 2 panics (jsr <undefined>, exit 101) and 1 silent pass (if <undefined>, exit 0), both booked as general. Root cause one not several: a register folds to Poison and Poison is the shape of a forward reference, so all 15 consumers deferred it; the discriminator is that no later pass defines it. Injection witness verified firsthand: 5,243 rows with 0 naming line 86 before, 5,244 with exactly one added line after. Over-fire guards checked on both binaries: a symbol named a0 still assembles, addressing modes untouched, genuine forward references still defer. sigil-frontend-as 494 passed / 0 failed on the merged tree. Byte gates did NOT run, 127 reference-dependent binaries unmeasured; .emp front end NOT examined, stated as a gap.

headline: A typo in a build switch was silently deleting the code it guarded, and the build still said it succeeded.
matters: If you wrote a condition around a block of code and the switch name was misspelled, renamed, or never defined, the assembler treated it as OFF, left the code out of the cartridge, and exited successfully. The bytes were identical to having deliberately turned it off, so there was nothing to notice: you would be looking at a ROM missing a feature you were sure you had compiled in. It now refuses and names the switch. Here the old assembler was in the right and we were wrong, which is the opposite of the case I sent you an hour ago. A crash was fixed alongside it: jumping to a name that does not exist killed the assembler with an internal error instead of telling you. And two more silent faults were found and written down rather than quietly fixed, one of which means seven places in Sonic 2 were dropping blocks of code for this exact reason.
detail: AS-UNDEFINED-SYM-PANIC-AND-SILENT-IF landed d9f00a3e, clearing argument banked 14824555, pushed. Fault 1: eval_if_expr unwrap_or(false), where false is a verdict; rept/while/org already refuse their unfoldable arguments. Fault 2: a three-stage join, the shipped CLI path never calls resolve_layout, so JmpJsrSym hit link()'s unreachable!; fixed in link() so every caller is covered. Design question answered by evidence and it INVERTED my assumption: sigil is the MORE permissive side (resolves forward references by iterating to a fixpoint; asl refuses four such shapes at exit 2), so keying the refusal on convergence is strictly weaker than the reference. Aeon risk the agent tagged was closed here two ways: measurement over the whole AS-routed surface (3 files, closure self-contained, zero firings, both game roots exit 0) and construction (all three old link() arms were unreachable!, so the change is strictly panic-to-diagnostic and cannot red a green build). Corpus 5,243 to 5,254, four classes appeared, none rose, none gone, before-only name set empty. Suite 4,598 passed 0 failed. Byte gates did NOT execute, 127 reference-dependent binaries.

headline: I held a finished piece of work because it would have made the assembler quieter, and sending it back turned out to be the most productive message of the day.
matters: The work implemented a counter Sonic 2 uses in twelve places, and it was good: the design was chosen by comparing actual bytes against the old assembler rather than by argument. But on one shape it took a loud refusal and made it total silence, and the thing being silenced was the author's own way of saying stop the build and tell the user. It was quieter than both the previous version and the tool we are replacing, so I held it and asked one narrow question. What came back was better than a fix. The agent showed that its own safety check had been meaningless (the error it was testing for could never fire in that test), that the problem was not pre-existing as it had reported but created by this very change, and that the obvious fix, copying the old assembler exactly, would have been a disaster: it would have cut the diagnostics on one game from fifty down to one. It also found a bug in its own fix, where an error could be blamed on the wrong file. All of that came from one message declining to accept a finished parcel.
detail: AS-MOMPASS-UNIMPLEMENTED landed f1673ba2, lessons 9228829b, pushed. Semantics: 1 on the first fixpoint iteration, 2 on every later one, chosen by byte comparison at the corpus's own `if MOMPASS=2` shape. asl pass count != our iteration count (differ both directions across 6 probes; 2 vs 4 on the corpus root), but no MOMPASS site in any of the three corpora emits a byte, so the divergence cannot bite. 12/12 sites agree. Held version was silent/exit 0 where master was loud/exit 1 and asl loud/exit 3. Agent's original control was confounded (fatal behind a Poison-folded condition, never executed). Faithful hard stop measured and rejected: s1disasm 50 located diagnostics to 1, skdisasm 2132 to 1. Shipped fix carries the fatal, deduped, strictly additive; verified here byte-identical stdout and stderr to the MOMPASS-only binary on the corpus. Span misattribution in the fix (inc/c.asm reported as inc/b.asm) found on disk and fixed; verified here. Corpus 5,254 to 5,247. Suite 4,613 passed 0 failed. Byte gates did NOT execute, 127 reference-dependent binaries.

headline: I ran the deep check that no piece of work today had run, and it found that something I approved this afternoon quietly broke four tests. The fix I was checking is fine; the older one is not.
matters: The operator ordering fix turned out to be much bigger than booked, so instead of arguing it was safe I rebuilt all four game ROMs with it: every one came out identical to the frozen checksums, and I proved the build really used the new tool rather than assuming it. But that deep check also runs a set of tests the quicker checks skip, and it came back with five failures. Four of them trace to a fix I approved earlier today, and I confirmed that by going back to the commit before it, where they all pass. My mistake was in the reasoning I used to clear that earlier fix: I checked the two places the game uses the affected file and concluded that covered everything. It did not. Our own test suite is a third user of that file and builds it a different way again, and my argument had no room for a third case. The fifth failure is a check that says a file is out of date while also reporting that nothing changed, so it is contradicting itself, and it fails without any of my work.
detail: AS-ANDAND-PRECEDENCE landed 33aeee96, red banked f991ad40, pushed. Byte gate PASSED: all four aeon shapes rebuilt with the new binary match the pins (1c09fbfc/819131, e2144057/840324, 11ebd7ab/96602, 9b0d2ce7/102818), freshness witnessed by staggered mtimes and by a bogus-SIGIL_BUILD control that fails the build. Strict suite: 4609 passed, 5 failed, exit 101. 4x diag_assert_vector attributed by bisection to d9f00a3e (15/0 at parent 742c7366); 1x pins_rs_is_current declares STALE with 0 changed pins and fails on master. Precedence parcel proven innocent by a master control over the same tree. Root of my error: enumerated aeon's three roots as the consuming end; sigil's own harness is a fourth consumer synthesizing a third context. Failing site debugger.asm:572, but the same condition standalone agrees with asl, so it is context-specific and NOT the obvious reading.

headline: My regression is fixed, and the bug turned out to be two months old rather than something I broke. The tests that caught it could not have told a good fix from a bad one.
matters: The four tests I broke this afternoon are green again, and the deep check on the final code now passes everything except one pre-existing check that contradicts itself. The interesting part is what the fix was. Asking the assembler for a piece of a string starting before the string begins was being refused outright; the old assembler answers it, so we were wrong. That refusal has been in the code since early July. What my change did was turn an accidentally-correct silence into a visibly-wrong complaint, which is how it finally became noticeable. The thing I want on record though is the agent's own warning: those four tests compare our assembler against ITSELF, not against the old one, so a plausible but wrong fix would also have turned them green while quietly disagreeing with the tool we are copying. Four tests going from red to green told us the breakage was gone and told us nothing about whether the repair was right. The real evidence is three new tests measured directly against the old assembler.
detail: AS-IF-REFUSAL-DIAG-VECTOR landed 34dad07c, resolution banked c884bce8, pushed. Over-fire, not a correct refusal; pos<0 guard from d59bab36 (2026-07-04), present at 742c7366 where tests passed. asl length law: avail=max(0,strlen-pos); len==0 all of avail, len<0 zero, len>0 min(len,avail). Negative pos has behaviour not semantics: strlen(substr("wxyz",-4,0))=8, longer than source; substr("a",-1000000,0) segfaults asl at exit 139. Fix models the unreadable prefix as NUL, which decides every comparison as asl does since an AS string cannot contain NUL. H2 (&& short-circuits) positively refuted: (0)&&(1/0) is a hard division-by-zero in asl. Merged-tree strict gate in 3 segments each with an end marker: 685/0, 382/1, 3549/0; total 4616 passed 1 failed, 406 result lines, 0 skip-banner lines. Two monolithic runs were killed; the first reached 88 percent with 0 failures, which is a clean run minus the end marker.

headline: The last failing check was correct and I was the cause. A change I made this morning moved a generator without regenerating what it generates.
matters: I had this booked as a broken check that fires while reporting nothing changed. It was not broken. It was saying two true things at once: the file really was out of date, and none of the actual values in it had moved. The cause was my own dash removal this morning. It correctly changed the words the tools say and correctly left code comments alone, but some of those words are used to WRITE the comments in an automatically generated file. So the generator started producing one wording while the checked-in copy still had the other. The general lesson is the one I want kept: after any sweep like that, the files to check are not just the ones matching your search, but every file that something else generates. And there is a matching case with no such check at all, which drifted silently and is booked. Regenerated rather than hand-edited, and I verified every one of the 108 changed lines is punctuation only with no number moving anywhere. The deep check on the whole tree is now completely clean.
detail: PINS-GATE-CONTRADICTS-ITSELF closed at d6ed3bec. Verdict came from a whole-text compare, count from a pin-level differ; both true. Cause: dash sweep f6618ec9 touched 38 lines of repin.rs which are string literals rendering comments into pins.rs, so the generator emitted the comma form while committed pins.rs kept 108 em-dash comment lines. Same root cause as GOLDEN-HEADER-UNGATED, which has no gate and drifted silently: one cause, two artifacts, loud vs silent purely by whether a currency check existed. Closed by regeneration per this repo's standing ruling; verified punctuation-only 108/108 with no hex constant on one side only. MERGED-TREE STRICT GATE NOW FULLY GREEN, segmented with end markers: sigil-cli 685/0, sigil-harness 383/0, other crates 3549/0, total 4617 passed 0 failed. Also booked: the failing gate's printed remediation does nothing without SIGIL_EMIT.

headline: Fixed a check that was right but unreadable, and found that a number I had not pinned down was already being used as evidence somewhere else.
matters: Yesterday's check told the truth in a way that read as nonsense: it said the file was out of date and that nothing had changed, because those two halves of the sentence were measuring different things. It now says which kind of drift it found and gives a command that actually works. Crucially I told the agent NOT to take the tidy fix, which would have been to make the check compare less until the sentence agreed with itself. That would have hidden the real problem it caught yesterday, and there is now a test that fails if anyone tries it. The part worth your attention: that confusing number had already been quoted in an unrelated note as proof that a change moved no bytes. The conclusion was right and the number offered for it was measuring something else entirely. A figure whose meaning nobody had pinned down became evidence in someone else's argument within hours of being printed.
detail: PINS-GATE-MESSAGE-MISLEADS landed 81d92f80, corrections 13960eb3, pushed. drift_report is now the single decision point for gate and binary and keeps whole-file strip_provenance equality; the_whole_file_verdict_survives_a_comment_only_drift reds under the narrowing mutation. Three red-first mutations from three anchors producing three different red sets (5/5, 6/4, 7/3), each shown applied and restored from a committed baseline. Strict gate 4,627 passed 0 failed, +10 over the 4,617 bar = the ten new tests. My repin claim was wrong a THIRD time: exit 2 naming SIGIL_EMIT holds only with AEON_DIR already set; with neither, exit 101 and SIGIL_EMIT appears zero times. Also corrected two files the agent flagged but declined on a mistaken ownership belief, both this lane's: OVERSEER.md's stale wording, and the if-refusal note reading 0 changed pins as positive byte evidence at two sites.

headline: Three generated files are back in step with what generates them, and there is now a check so they cannot drift silently again. Also fixed a check I had broken this afternoon without noticing.
matters: These three were the quiet version of yesterday's noisy failure: same cause, and the only reason nobody spotted them is that nothing was watching. They are regenerated rather than hand-edited, and every measured row in them is proven unchanged, with the proof itself tested by deliberately corrupting a row to confirm it objects. The new check is built so it fails if the generator moves and the files do not, which is the failure that actually happened. Separately and more usefully: a check that is supposed to run on every landing has been failing since this afternoon because of something I landed, and I never saw it because I have been running the tests directly instead of the script that wraps them. Both things that escaped today escaped through that same gap. And my first attempt at fixing it made the tool happy while quietly changing what a paragraph in the code says, which I caught only by reading the surrounding text rather than trusting the green.
detail: GOLDEN-HEADER-UNGATED landed c30179d5, clippy fix and lesson 0ad78371, pushed. Body md5 identical per file across regeneration (121/177/2164 rows), 0 changed lines outside the header, prover shown non-blind. asl md5 61e6725... with exit status checked, all three generators exit 0, and each already asserts success per invocation so the generator's zero carries all 523 asl runs. Gate derives from header() rather than duplicating PREAMBLE; 4 mutations red-first, the load-bearing one being PREAMBLE perturbed with artifacts untouched (3/3 red). Measured scope limit banked in the module doc: provenance values round-trip, so a lie about which build answered survives. Strict 4,631/0. Clippy was exit 101 on master from 392503fe (mine, this afternoon); first fix indented six lines and went green while folding a paragraph into an unrelated bullet, corrected to end the list.

headline: The assembler now knows 21 sound-processor instructions it did not, and the agent found a soundness hole that would have opened silently if it had only added the instructions.
matters: Sonic 2's sound driver uses one of these 17 times, so it could not assemble past them. The valuable part is what the agent noticed on its own. There is a checker that verifies a routine preserves the registers it promises to preserve, and when it meets an instruction it does not recognise it assumes that instruction writes NOTHING. That is the dangerous direction: teach the assembler a new instruction without also teaching that checker, and a routine that really does clobber registers passes a check that says it does not. It landed both together. It also enumerated by going through the processor's opcode space rather than working from a list of names, which is why it caught an instruction with a real use that no name-based search would have found.
detail: AS-Z80-INSTRUCTION-COVERAGE landed 6bdf8d86, verification findings cf53ad2b, pushed. Enumerated over the opcode space: 612 forms, one asl invocation each, byte coverage checked back per page (base 252/252, CB 248/256, ED 56/80). Gap 55 refused forms / 28 mnemonics; after, 8 DD/FD index forms, zero sites, left deliberately. z80_preserves::z80_writes_regs falls through to vec![], verified here, and the ldir arm's own comment named this kill condition; write-set arms land in the same commit as the encoders. Row corrections: count is 21 not 22 (sll has no asl answer under any spelling); ldi was NOT the only live form, sbc hl,bc has one site at s2.sounddriver.asm:4023; reti/retn were already priced at 14 T with no encoder. Corpus 5,247 to 5,229, no class rose or appeared. Landing run through the script: 410 suites, 4,650 passed, 0 failed, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, RESULT GREEN, reconciling as 4,631 + 19 new. Spot-checked five encodings against asl here: all byte-identical.

headline: I overflowed the size limit on the document every session reads at startup, which was failing a test. Cut back under it, and reclaimed 49 GB of dead agent workspaces on the way out.
matters: That document has a hard size limit because every session pays to read it before doing anything. I spent the day writing findings into it and crossed the limit partway through without noticing, then kept writing. Every entry was real; the file was just the wrong home for most of them. It is now a third smaller, with nothing shaved: the short rules stay and the stories behind them moved to the history file. The instruction I gave for proving nothing was lost was itself wrong for this kind of move, and the agent caught that rather than bending its work until the tool went quiet. It proved the tool was objecting to text that was already there by running the same check against the unsplit state. Separately, 49 GB of finished agent workspaces were sitting locked; I checked each one held no unsaved work before removing it, and kept the seven branches that are not yet merged.
detail: BOOT-DOC-CUT landed bf76b8b3. docs/OVERSEER.md 105,389 to 66,177 B, headroom 33,823, no residual. the_boot_read_is_inside_its_byte_bound red on master, now green; companion the_bound_actually_refuses_something proves the bound can still fail. Landing run through scripts/landing-run.sh on the merged tree: 410 suites, 4,650 passed, 0 failed, 0 FAILED lines, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, CARGO_EXIT 0, reconciles 4650+0, LANDING_EXIT 0. My prescribed three-output prover invocation is wrong for an append-style cut (compares 1,226 original lines against 7,274); reproduced here as an order-preserving partition failure. Correct form uses fragments of exactly what moved: PROVED, 1226 = 710 boot + 300 log + 216 reference, tokens delta 0. Verified here that both siblings are pure appends by byte-identical prefix at 446,869 and 60,875. Housekeeping: 31 worktrees/127 GB to 13/76 GB, 49 GB reclaimed; every removed tree verified 0 tracked-dirty, 0 untracked, tip in master; locks cleared with git worktree unlock, never a second -f. Branches 246 to 17, the 7 unmerged kept and named.

headline: The assembler's listing now states, for every symbol, whether an address is where the code runs or where it is stored. Three separate attempts to work that out from the source got it wrong first.
matters: Five engine tools each try to figure this out for themselves, and nobody could establish how many get it right, because you cannot tell the two kinds of address apart by looking at them. That is the whole problem: a sound-processor label running at one address and an engine routine stored at the same address are the same four digits. The engine lane tried to count the affected symbols by address range and got engine routines instead, which is exactly the mistake the marker prevents, made by someone who had just been warned about it. Their broader belief about where the phasing lives is refuted by their own source file. And my own claim that started this, that five tools re-derive it and one is right, had no measurement behind it anywhere and I withdrew it. The assembler now simply says which is which, so nobody has to guess. It found six such symbols in the main game and two in the demo. One thing I got wrong and want on record: I told the agent the listing had four consumers, and missed the one that builds the debug symbol table into the actual cartridge, so this could have moved ROM bytes. It did not, and that is measured rather than assumed.
detail: EMIT-LISTING-PHASED-MARKER landed 64b843ae. Section emitted unconditionally with a count, rows only for phased symbols, VMA and LMA both on the row. Population derived from sections (vma_origin != lma and image_len > 0): 6 per sonic4 shape, 2 in demo, no shipped shape unphased, so the count-0 case was CONSTRUCTED. Cross-check against aeon's 36-name source derivation: wrong both directions, 29 in no listing, misses one demo carries. Five grammars proved before/after with extracted values, not agreement alone. Full-ROM byte gate verified here on the branch (native_full_sonic4_plain and _debug, with deb2_appendix_negative_controls). Merged-tree landing run: 411 suites, 4,658 passed, 0 failed, 0 FAILED lines, 0 skip lines, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, reconciles 4658+0, LANDING_EXIT 0.

headline: The old assembler can report a complete-looking failure while never having looked for a whole class of problem. Two of our recorded findings turned out to be that, and one of them described a difference that does not exist.
matters: If a file has any mistake in it, the old assembler stops after the first pass and never runs the one that finds undefined names, so it reports a plausible failure with a plausible error count while having never gone looking. It says so, in a sentence at the bottom of a printout that no script reads. Our tool now records, on every run, whether the assembler actually looked, not just whether it failed. Then we swept all 348 test files we have: 24 were affected. Two of them had conclusions that were actually wrong because of it. One recorded a silent wrong answer that was really a suppressed one; the other recorded a difference between our assembler and the old one that simply is not there, and I checked that one myself. The rest coexist with the problem without depending on it, and saying so is part of the finding rather than a hedge.
detail: ASL-PASS-LOOP-SWALLOWS-DIAGNOSTICS landed 0ff11de8. Merged-tree landing run: 411 suites, 4,658 passed, 0 failed, 0 FAILED lines, 0 skip lines, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, reconciles 4658+0, LANDING_EXIT 0. Position is irrelevant, not first-error as the row said. Console never carries the warning; it is -L footer only, which decided where detection could live. THREE states not two: absence of the warning is not completeness, since a fatal or crash writes a footerless listing and 18 probes are that shape. Sweep of 348 tracked .asm: 24 INCOMPLETE, 91 failing WITH complete diagnostics, so a failure-keyed check fires on 115 where 24 are affected. Sub-finding: m17/p3/p5 ran two passes reporting #1010 then refused a third, so reported-undefined-symbols is not evidence of completeness. Corrections: as-struct-dots q8 and irp-irpc-argcount p2, the latter verified at this seat (ARGCOUNT alone: exit 2, 2 passes, symbol undefined, no byte column). My brief wrongly claimed the mechanism was new; a note landed the same day already named it and booked this sweep.

headline: A check I have been prescribing all week compares almost nothing. It reported perfect agreement because the thing it compares does not exist in the files it reads.
matters: We have a sweep that assembles every file in four reference disassemblies with the old tool and the new one and compares the results. It has been reporting a clean match, and I have asked for it three times as proof that a change moved no bytes. It emits no bytes at all: those files are fragments meant to be included into a program, not programs, so 1,751 of 1,753 produce nothing to compare. The match was real about error messages and meaningless about bytes, and I had written it up as being about bytes. The thing that caught it was a rule I adopted a few hours earlier from the engine lane: say what each side actually produced, not just that the two agreed. It caught an instrument I had prescribed myself. The real byte check was run separately and properly and does hold.
detail: AS-SET-OPENS-SCOPE landed 0b06a188, findings banked d0019918, pushed. Twelve binder spellings diverged not one, 24 of 28 matrix rows, all agree now. The row's five cited sites are dotted binders and CANNOT diverge; the nine real sites are in four other files and none diverges, so this closed a silent wrong answer the corpus does not ask for and moved no byte. Sweep vacuity verified independently here: 0 of 40 s2disasm .asm files emit any bytes standalone; both arms accepted 2 of 1,753 and emitted 0 bytes; DIFFER=0 covers 43,862 diagnostic lines. Narrows the strict-args null result's byte wording, not its conclusion. sweep.sh now prints the byte census and refuses a zero-byte run reading as byte identity. Real byte half: both aeon shapes on both binaries, 1c09fbfc/819131 and e2144057/840324, cmp identical, 1,659,455 bytes emitted. Landing run 412 suites, 4,670 passed, 0 failed, GREEN.

headline: The timing analyser can now price every sound-processor instruction the assembler can emit, and the check I asked for would have missed most of the gap.
matters: We taught the assembler 21 new instructions tonight; the part that works out how long code takes knew the cost of none of them, and answered Unknown, which was the safe direction. Now it prices them all. Three things I specified were wrong and each would have caused a defect. I asked for a check that fails when an INSTRUCTION has no cost; that is too coarse, because an instruction can be priced for some operand shapes and not others, and the coarse version would have declared the job done with 320 forms still unpriced. I said sixteen block instructions carry two costs; only eight do, and treating the others that way would have made the analyser refuse instructions whose cost is a simple constant. And the real hazard was not in the table at all: pricing the call instruction CORRECTLY would have let the span calculator add up straight through a call and report a wrong total from entirely right numbers. One instruction was already doing that.
detail: ISA-CYCLE-TABLE-GAP landed 49a84f26. Population DERIVED FROM THE ENCODER, not a list: 320 unpriced forms over 51 mnemonics against the row's 21; the vocabulary is macro-expanded into both the walked vector and an exhaustive match on the encoder enum, so a new variant fails to COMPILE. Verified here that master priced inc for reg8/pair/index-pair and not for (hl) or (ix+d), so a mnemonic-level guard would have passed. CycleBail::OpaqueCall lands in the same commit as the call price, closing a pre-existing hole where rst was already summing silently. Three left Unknown deliberately, all because the encoder cannot emit those bytes. Eight repeating block ops give [cycles.ambiguous-branch] its first reachable input, its doc having claimed none existed from an enumeration of terminators. Merged-tree gate segmented after two kills, each segment with its own end marker: sigil-cli 685/0, rest 3,998/0, total 412 result lines, 4,683 passed, 0 failed, 0 skip-banner lines so the strict gates genuinely ran.

headline: I broke another team's build by refreshing a shared tool while they were using it, and the rule I wrote this morning is what let me do it.
matters: There is one copy of the assembler that every tool here links against. It had gone out of date, so I rebuilt it. Another lane's agent was midway through a four-part build with the old version's fingerprint recorded in its instructions, so two of its parts would have been built by one assembler and two by another, with nothing in the result saying so. That is a false claim of identical output, which is exactly what the fingerprint existed to prevent. Hours earlier I had written a rule saying this shared tool needs a named owner allowed to update it, or it goes stale. I became that owner, and the first time I used it I caused this, because the rule said who may touch it and nothing about when. A rule that assigns ownership without a coordination point does not remove the danger, it moves it. The old copy is gone and cannot be recovered. The other lane is restarting its work under the new version, and the rule now says the hub opens a window after asking everyone who builds against that path.
detail: Swap at 2026-09-06 05:45:48Z, md5 945387f2 (d094c3c8) to fa18ebfe (e6e942e5). Admitted within a minute of the hub's amendment arriving, twice, our messages crossing. Previous binary unrecoverable: no copy in scratch or .pinned, and a rebuild of the revision is a different artifact by this repo's own rule, so it was not offered as a restoration. Hub ruled e6e942e5 stays, no swap back, no rebuild, path frozen to this lane until its word. Every check I ran before swapping was about the artifact (staleness, provenance, nothing pinning the old digest in tracked files, standing .pinned untouched) and none was about the other lanes. Prophylactic banked: copy the outgoing binary aside BEFORE the rename. Hub rule supersedes my amendment because a lane cannot see who is mid-run and only the hub can.

headline: The assignment fix landed, and my instruction for it named a route difference that does not exist while contradicting a row that was right.
matters: Assigning a name to something that does not exist is now refused where you wrote it, on all five spellings and every route. Two separate causes, where I told the agent there was one: one family recorded nothing at all and was silent even in the real game build, the other recorded the problem properly and one route simply never read it. And the fix I specified could not be taken: evaluating the expression where it is written would refuse the cross-language definitions the real build depends on, because at that point the assembler cannot tell a name that will never exist from one the linker is about to supply. I reached my wrong conclusion by running the tool two ways that turn out to be the same code path, varied only by an output format flag.
detail: AS-ASSIGN-UNRESOLVED landed 62057594, route lesson banked 0eb20272. Two causes: directive_set had no else arm so set/:=/eval recorded nothing on any route; equ/= deferred properly and the .asm CLI stopped at link() rather than resolve_layout, verified at e6e942e5 main.rs:124 against seams at 436/789/902. Fix is one shared defer_unresolved_assign for five spellings plus routing the single-file CLI through resolve_layout. Forward references proven not to fire across five shapes, each arm ASL_DIAG complete, asserting no symbolic obligation survives the front end before comparing bytes. Sweep measured diagnostics and zero bytes (0 of 1,828 accepted); bytes measured by the landing run's seven shipped-shape CRC gates, all unchanged. Landing 412 suites, 4,689 passed, 0 failed. Now dispatched AS-FLOAT-FREQ-TABLE, where the row is again wrong on count, place and mechanism: 23 not 84, two sites not a note table, and asl's log is base 10 so a natural-log implementation gives 4 where the reference gives 2.

headline: The assembler can now compute the logarithm Sonic 2 needs, and most of what the row blamed on floating point was a missing generated file.
matters: The row said 84 complaints from a note table computed in floating point. It is six, at one place, and no note table is involved: a heads-up-display counter works out how many digits a number has by taking a logarithm, which our assembler did not have. The other seventeen I had attributed to floating point were nothing of the kind. They come from a file the build generates and which was simply absent; running the generation step alone, with no change to the assembler at all, makes them disappear. My own small test had hidden that by supplying a value for the very thing whose absence was the fault, so it tested a program in which the problem cannot happen. The trap I warned about was real and there was a finer one underneath it: the old assembler's logarithm is base ten, which I flagged, but computing base ten the obvious way from natural logarithms gives a number a fraction below three, which rounds down to two and emits a different byte. A wrong base is loud. A wrong way of computing the right base is one byte in one place.
detail: AS-FLOAT-FREQ-TABLE landed 344ebf6d, three findings banked 6017f168. Site 2 isolated as build-generated sound/DAC/generated/*.inc absent: generation half of build.lua alone takes corpus 5,229 to 5,168, cannot-include 39 to 0, float 23 to 6, with no sigil change; confirmed on Sonic 1 under the unchanged master binary. Verified here: directory absent, 39 cannot-include rows. int() FLOORS (INT(-3.2) = -4; INT(LOG(0.5)*1e6) = -301030 vs -301029 truncating). Bases from exit-0 ASL_DIAG-complete listings: exact log10, natural ln, exp e^x, trig radians, abs type-preserving. Hub's premise wrong: Plan 5 float machinery not reusable by the AS front end. Half-fix caught: abs took S1 rept failures 8 to 4 and the 4 were exactly the ascending sites, unary plus missing. Hardening: floor_to_i64 saturated so int(1e30) emitted i64::MAX. Corpus float 6 to 0, six lines removed zero added; S1 57 to 49. Landing 412 suites, 4,700 passed, 0 failed.

headline: The alignment change I have been calling unfinished has been finished since 30 August, and my own briefing document kept telling every new session otherwise.
matters: Nothing was broken by it, but for a week every fresh session here started its day believing a finished piece of work was still waiting, and could have spent a day redoing it. It only came to light because another team asked which pieces were done and I checked the code instead of reading my own page. The fix is a habit rather than a tool: when a job finishes, the note that told us to do it gets corrected in the same breath, because nothing anywhere checks that.
detail: R7 alignment flip landed e2517405 2026-08-30, verified ancestor of master; packing walk reads align_up(running, required_for(head label)); packed_align_of absent from all Rust source; frozen chain 196 (seven shapes shrink). docs/OVERSEER.md R7 block said 'what remains is the flip itself' until e5b47915. Same instance class as the banked snapshot-as-standing-fact rule, in the document that banks it.

headline: The number this project has steered by for weeks was counting the assembler plus a missing step of the disassembly's own build, and could not tell them apart.
matters: Every piece of work in the Sonic 2 project has been sized off one count of complaints. The community disassemblies build some of their own source files from sound data at build time, and a plain checkout does not have them, so the count included the assembler's real faults AND the noise from files that were simply absent. Running each disassembly's own build step first and re-measuring: Sonic 2 drops 61, Sonic 1 drops 7, S3K drops 44, and nothing anywhere gets worse. Two things worth knowing beyond the fix. The old number was not wrong, it was two things read as one, and it reconciles exactly once you separate them, so nothing anyone concluded from it has to be thrown away, and I had that checked rather than assumed. And the reason this went unnoticed for so long is that the usual way we prove which version of a tree we measured cannot see it at all: a prepared tree and a bare one look identical to it. The measuring tool now refuses to produce a number over an unprepared tree instead of quietly producing a smaller one.
detail: Merged 387042f2 (branch parcel/corpus-generated-includes, tip b95a5334). Restated baselines, sigil md5 93b368052dbb77a5d2c199134f9c002d, each corpus in its own detached worktree, dirty 0: s2disasm e45ebf33 bare 5,223 -> prepared 5,162 (-61: 39 cannot-include, 17 float, 3 unresolved symbol, 2 unresolved if); s1disasm f6ece657 49 -> 42; skdisasm 2fcd861 2,170 -> 2,126. DELTAS SURVIVE, measured: Z80-coverage parcel rebuilt at base c38b44fd and tip 6bdf8d86 over a prepared tree reads 5,186 -> 5,168, same -18, same two classes, name sets identical both directions. Two readiness gates, both derived not listed, independence measured in both directions, both proved red with the mutation shown applied on disk (ls says gone / stat says mode 0) and restored from the corpus's own generator. headline: CORRECTION to two earlier entries: the complaint counts I gave you in them were inflated by the same missing build step, and here are the right ones.
matters: Two entries of mine quote counts that were measured over an unprepared tree. The conclusions in both are unaffected, because what those entries actually turned on was the CHANGE between two numbers and that change is unchanged, but the absolute figures are wrong and would mislead anyone who quoted them later. Appending the correction rather than editing the old entries: this is a dated record of what was said when, and quietly restating a past number is the move that makes a record untrustworthy even when the new number is the right one.

Both endpoints in both entries moved by exactly 61, the corpus build-system constant. Correction established by 387042f2; method in docs/superpowers/notes/2026-09-06-corpus-generated-includes.md. The agent that found this deliberately did not rewrite the entries and routed them here, which was the right call.

headline: A warning the assembler raised early used to be thrown away, on reasoning that turned out to be false, and I checked it against the real assembler rather than trusting the note.
matters: When the assembler works out a program it goes over the source several times. If it complained on an early pass and not the last one, that complaint vanished. The note explaining why said the real assembler reprints its complaints each time round, so a later pass genuinely replaces an earlier one. That is not what it does: it prints the union of everything it found on any pass, so nothing was ever being replaced and we were simply losing warnings. Confirmed by running the real assembler myself on a test case, and by running our old and new builds side by side: the old one prints nothing, the new one prints the warning at the same place. The honest limit: across all three of the community disassemblies there are thirteen places that could raise a warning and none of them currently does, so this fix is right but nothing in the real corpus exercises it yet.
detail: Landed df49f065 (branch tip c2819fb3), pushed. asl md5 61e672562465725a8c102288a7da9098, exit 0, probe with `if MOMPASS=1` guard: prints cw1.asm(4): warning. Arms distinct by md5 (BEFORE a466e83b, AFTER 354a6db4): 0 lines vs 1 line at the same file/line. Corpus delta +0/+0/+0, 13 warning sites 0 firings, 12 of 13 reached, instrument proved on a planted canary. Byte-neutral: Level::Warning never reaches the module, both shipped shapes rebuilt and matched golden. Landing run on the MERGED tree: 412 suites, 4704 passed, 0 failed, 2 ignored, 0 skip lines, CARGO_EXIT 0, CLIPPY_EXIT 0, aggregate reconciled independently at this seat. NOT run: the script's own --baseline reconciliation, because I did not state one. message is booked not implemented; the old row pairing it with warning was wrong, a message is dropped on every pass including the converged one.

headline: Two more places where the assembler quietly gives a wrong answer instead of complaining, found by accident while doing the above.
matters: Both are the kind this project keeps hitting and cannot see: the count of complaints we steer by shows nothing wrong, because a wrong answer is silent. The worse of the two: on the Sonic 1 disassembly our assembler thinks the sound driver is about sixty times bigger than it is, and refuses the file over it. The real assembler builds the same tree cleanly and reports the true size. Because our refusal stops that pass dead, nine further places in that file are never reached at all, so it looks like one complaint while actually costing ten. The other is a piece of text formatting that silently comes back unfinished. Both are now queue items rather than buried in a ledger.
detail: AS-S1-DRIVER-SIZE-60X: s1disasm sound/z80.asm(229), sigil says 73DFDh, asl exits 0 and its own message reports 1BC6h. fatal sets aborted, truncating the pass: 9 of 12 message sites and 1 of 9 warning sites unreached. Hypothesis, untested: phase/org accounting, not emit size. Size off a PREPARED tree only (bare gives 72325h). AS-MESSAGE-AND-INTERPOLATION: message discarded on every pass; \{(EndOfRom-StartOfRom)/1024.0} returns uninterpolated, and that idiom is how all five s2disasm table-size messages are written.

headline: The document every session reads at startup grew past its size limit today, so I moved nine rules out of it rather than shortening any of them.
matters: There is a hard limit on that document because every session pays to read it, and a gate fails the whole test run when it is exceeded. It fired today, which is the gate working. Your standing rule is that the fix is to move closed material out, never to trim a rule to fit, and I followed that: nine blocks moved word for word into the companion document that gets read at the moment each rule applies, with the startup document naming all nine where they used to sit. It went from about 99KB to about 86KB, so this should hold for a while. I could not get a clean PROVED from the checking tool, and I am not dressing that up: the tool assumes one document splitting apart, while this was a move between two documents that both already existed. Everything that matters came out exact.

Cut 43caf427: 98,857 -> 85,629 B, nine contiguous moment-read blocks verbatim to OVERSEER-REFERENCE.md, all nine named in the pointer (verified with a canaried matcher after two false results from hasty ones). prove_doc_split.py against the UNION of both files at master: 1a absent 0, 1b undeclared 0, 1c over-declared 0, token delta 0, heading-aware seams introduced 0.
